title: Lessons Learned from CZII’s Kaggle CryoET Object Identification Challenge
content: Cryo-electron tomography (cryoET) is a powerful technique for visualizing cellular structure with molecular detail. When sufficient copies of a target molecule can be identified across multiple tomograms, these copies can be aligned and averaged to resolve the molecule’s structure in situ. This process of subtomogram averaging (STA) can reach subnanometer resolution and reveal conformational ensembles. However, locating sufficient individual molecules in the crowded environment of the cell remains a significant bottleneck that impedes the routine use of STA. Machine learning (ML) algorithms are well-suited to overcome this annotation bottleneck by delivering solutions that are more efficient and versatile than the traditional approach of template matching [1]. Though numerous ML particle picking methods have recently been developed [2-4], the fact that the field has not coalesced behind a single approach suggests that these algorithms do not generalize sufficiently well to serve the community’s diverse needs. To spur innovation, CZII launched a three-month CryoET Object Identification Challenge hosted by Kaggle that tasked contestants with developing ML algorithms for multi-class particle picking [5-6]. Contestants were provided with seven labeled training tomograms that contained five particles of interest in addition to non-target particles and structural features that tend to confound picking algorithms. The submissions were then scored against hundreds of labeled but unseen tomograms from the same dataset. To encourage generalizability, the target particles were selected for their diverse shapes and large range of molecular weights. To promote applicability, the benchmark dataset was designed to balance the competing needs of a realistic sample that contains artifacts inherent to experimental tomograms but is still feasible to label with high confidence. Participation was high with 1135 contestants, many of whom were ML experts with no prior experience in volumetric imaging. In this talk, I will compare the top-scoring algorithms to previously developed methods and describe the impact of picking accuracy on downstream tasks like STA. This analysis has underscored the difficulty of evaluating pick quality and highlighted the need for more sophisticated methods to improve data curation [7].
